questions.q: A loan type has approved: boolean, rejected: boolean, approvedBy?: string and rejectionReason?: string. The business has three real states. What is the core problem?
questions.explain: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 shapes for 3 states. Every reader must guess which combinations are real. A discriminated union allows exactly the three real states.
options: The type allows sixteen combinations, most of which (approved and rejected, approved with no approver) are impossible in the business

questions.q: Thinking of types as sets of values, which statement is right?
questions.explain: A literal type is a set with one value; a union puts sets together. never is the empty set, and "in both" describes an intersection, A & B.
options: "pending" | "approved" is the set containing exactly those two strings
never is the set of all values
A | B contains only values that are in both A and B

questions.q: Why does amount.toFixed(2) fail to compile when amount: number | string?
questions.explain: The value might be a string, so TypeScript refuses a number-only method until you narrow, for example with typeof amount === "number".
options: Because on a union you may only use what every member supports, and strings have no toFixed

questions.q: Given type Status = "pending" | "approved", which assignment is an error?
questions.explain: A member fits the union, and a union fits any wider type. But a union does not fit one of its members: someStatus might be "pending". Narrow first.

questions.q: What makes a union of object types a discriminated union?
questions.explain: A shared property with distinct literal types (status: "pending", status: "approved", …) lets TypeScript narrow to exactly one member when you check it.
options: Every member has a different number of properties
Every member has the same property (the discriminant) holding a different literal type

questions.q: Why does narrowing stop working if the discriminant is typed status: string in every member?
questions.explain: The discriminant must be a literal type in each member. With string, the check tells TypeScript nothing about which member it has.
options: Because strings cannot be compared with ===
Because checking status === "approved" no longer rules out any member: every member allows every string
It still works the same way

questions.q: What does TypeScript report for this, where LoanRequest is the pending/approved/rejected union?
questions.explain: TypeScript uses the discriminant to pick the member you meant, PendingLoan, and then checks the object literal against it alone. The extra property is caught.
questions.code: const loan: LoanRequest = { id: 3, customer: "Chidi", amount: 20000, status: "pending", approvedBy: "Tunde" };
options: Nothing, because approvedBy exists on another member
That approvedBy does not exist in type PendingLoan

questions.q: Why is function approve(loan: PendingLoan, officer: string): ApprovedLoan better than function approve(loan: LoanRequest, officer: string): LoanRequest?
questions.explain: The parameter type encodes where the move may start, and the return type where it ends. Passing a rejected loan is a compile error, and the result has approvedBy without further checks.
options: The compiler rejects approving a loan that is not pending, and callers know they get an approved loan back
It avoids the need for a discriminant

questions.q: Why build a new object in approve instead of writing loan.status = "approved"?
questions.explain: A state change usually adds or removes fields. Building a complete new object of the target member keeps every value valid. Making the discriminant readonly stops the in-place change at compile time.
options: Because objects cannot be changed in JavaScript
Changing only the status leaves a half-changed object: an "approved" loan with no approver or approval date
Because new objects use less memory

questions.q: What does an assertNever(loan) call in the default branch give you that a plain default: return "" does not?
questions.explain: When every member is handled, loan is never in the default branch and the call compiles. A forgotten member is not never, so the call fails to compile. At runtime, the throw turns silent wrong answers into visible errors.
options: A compile error naming any member you forgot, and a thrown error at runtime if unexpected data (such as an unknown status from a database) reaches it
It makes the switch run faster

questions.q: A switch over a union has no default, every case returns, and the function's return type is string. A new member is added. What happens?
questions.explain: It is exhaustive, but indirectly: the error points at the return type, not at the switch, and it only works while every case returns.
options: Nothing; the switch simply does not match it
TS2366: the function can now reach its end without returning, which the string return type does not allow
The new member is sent to the first case
The compiler adds a default case

questions.q: How does const colour: Record<LoanStatus, string> = { … } act as an exhaustive check?
questions.explain: Record<K, V> requires a property for every key in K. It suits mappings from each member to a value, but has no runtime safety net: an unexpected key reads as undefined.
options: It throws at runtime for missing keys
Every member of LoanStatus is a required key, so leaving one out is a compile error (TS2741)
It is not exhaustive at all

questions.q: Why is an if / else if / else chain over a status union risky when members are added later?
questions.explain: The code keeps compiling and treats the new member like whatever the else was written for. A switch with assertNever turns that into a compile error.
options: The final else silently takes every member you did not name, including new ones, so nobody is forced to decide how they should be handled
Because TypeScript does not narrow in else branches

questions.q: What is the type "pending" | "approved" | string equal to?
questions.explain: A set united with a bigger set that contains it is just the bigger set. Misspellings like "aproved" then compile. Model open-ended values as their own member instead, for example { status: "other"; label: string }.
options: The three-member union, with string as a fallback for autocomplete
Just string: every literal is already a string, so the union collapses and the literal checks disappear

questions.q: Why does if (loan.approvedBy) fail to compile on the loan union?
questions.explain: Rule 1 again: only what every member supports. Check the discriminant, loan.status === "approved", and then approvedBy is available.
options: Because approvedBy is a string and cannot be used in if
Because approvedBy exists only on the approved member, and you cannot read a property that some members do not have before narrowing
Because truthiness checks are banned in strict mode

questions.q: Why return a TransferResult union instead of throwing when a transfer is declined for insufficient funds?
questions.explain: A thrown error is invisible in the function's type, and catch receives unknown. A result union lists every outcome. Keep exceptions for the unexpected: a crashed database, a bug.
options: Throwing is not allowed in TypeScript
A decline is an expected business outcome: putting it in the return type makes every caller handle it, with typed data about why
Unions are faster than exceptions in every case
Because catch cannot catch errors from async code

questions.q: In TransferError, why does the "insufficient-funds" member carry balance and requested, while "account-frozen" carries nothing?
questions.explain: The same principle as the loan states: data belongs to the case it describes. The message function can then say "You have ₦30000, but tried to send ₦45000" without optional fields.
options: By accident; every member should have the same fields
Each error member carries exactly the data needed to explain that case, and nothing that does not apply
Because frozen accounts have no balance
Because unions cannot have empty members

questions.q: For object types, what is Loan & Audit?
questions.explain: An intersection keeps values that belong to both sets. For objects that means having every property of both. If Loan is a union, the intersection applies to each member.
options: A value that is either a loan or an audit record
A value with all the properties of Loan and all the properties of Audit
Only the properties the two types have in common
A compile error unless both are interfaces

questions.q: Loan is Pending | Approved. What is Loan & Audit equivalent to?
questions.explain: Intersection spreads over union like multiplication over addition. Each member gains the audit fields, and the union stays discriminated.

questions.q: What is the type of id in { id: number } & { id: string }?
questions.explain: Intersections combine property by property, and number & string is empty. No object can satisfy the type. When you see an unexpected never, look for intersected types that disagree.
options: never, because no value is both a number and a string

questions.q: What does TypeScript reduce { status: "pending" } & { status: "approved" } to?
questions.explain: When two object types disagree on a literal property that acts as a discriminant, TypeScript reduces the whole intersection to never.
options: { status: never }, which can still hold an empty object
never: the whole object type is empty

questions.q: What does Extract<Loan, { status: "pending" }> give you?
questions.explain: Extract picks union members that are assignable to the second type. It avoids repeating the member's definition. Like every type, it is erased at runtime.
options: The members of the Loan union that fit { status: "pending" }: the pending member
A loan with its status removed
A runtime function that filters pending loans

questions.q: A client sends { "status": "approved", "approvedBy": "me", "amount": 900000 } to your create-loan endpoint. The handler's parameter is typed LoanRequest. What protects you?
questions.explain: The body arrives at runtime, long after compiling. Validate the input, and never let a client set a field that staff should set: a new loan is always created as pending by your code.
options: The discriminated union: TypeScript rejects it
Nothing, unless you validate at runtime and ignore the client's status entirely: types do not check incoming JSON

questions.q: This uses the old boolean model. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both nonsense loans compile. Loan 1 is both approved and rejected, and the order of the ifs decides it is "rejected". Loan 2 is approved with no approver. A discriminated union makes both impossible to write.
options:
#1 approved by Ngozi
#2 approved by undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The number branch multiplies directly. In the second branch amount is a string, so replace is allowed; removing the comma gives "1200.75", which becomes 120075 kobo.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The two cases without a return between them share one branch, so "disbursed" falls into the "approved" code: 1.5% of 40000 is 600.

questions.q: A status from an old database bypasses the types. What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse returns any, so "on-hold" reaches label unchecked. No case matches, and assertNever throws with the bad value, instead of the function quietly returning undefined.

questions.q: A "frozen" status was added last week. What does this print?
questions.explain: The else swallows "frozen", so a frozen account can withdraw, and the compiler said nothing. An exhaustive switch would have forced a decision.
options: It does not compile: "frozen" is not handled

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 200 is under the ₦500 minimum, 3000 leaves 2000, and 9000 is more than the balance. After checking r.ok, TypeScript knows which member you have, so r.balance and r.error are each only read where they exist.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each status looks up its own colour, in the order of the statuses array.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The intersection added createdBy to both members, so it can be read without narrowing. approvedBy still needs the status check.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The filter keeps the two pending loans. The l is Pending return type (a type guard, covered in Narrowing) tells TypeScript the result is a Pending[].

questions.q: Replace the boolean model with a discriminated union of pending, approved (with approvedBy) and rejected (with reason), and rewrite describe with a switch. Print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: Each state carries only its own data, and inside each case TypeScript knows which fields exist. An approved loan without an approver no longer compiles.
questions.expected:
#1 pending
#2 approved by Ngozi
#3 rejected: income too low

questions.q: Write approve(loan: Pending, officer: string): Approved that builds a new approved loan. Print the result's status and approver: approved Ngozi.
questions.explain: The parameter type says where the move may start, the return type where it ends. Because every field is readonly, the function must build a complete new object.

questions.q: Add the missing "disbursed" case (fee: 1% of the amount, rounded) and an assertNever default. Print 0 450 800.
questions.explain: The starter's default: return 0 silently charged disbursed loans nothing. With assertNever, the compiler reports any member that reaches the default, and the runtime throws on unknown data.

questions.q: Make transfer return a result union instead of throwing: { ok: true; newBalance: number } or { ok: false; error: "frozen" | "insufficient-funds" }. Print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: Every outcome is now in the return type, so a caller cannot read newBalance without first checking ok. The errors are a literal union, so a message table or switch over them can be exhaustive.

questions.q: Write a Record that maps every DeclineReason to a customer message, and print the message for each reason in the list.
questions.explain: A Record keyed by the union requires one message per reason, so adding a fourth reason is a compile error until someone writes its message.
questions.expected:
This card has expired.
Not enough funds on this card.

questions.q: Define type Audited = Loan & { createdBy: string; createdAt: string } and write trail(loan: Audited) that prints who created the loan and, for approved loans, who approved it.
questions.explain: The intersection spreads over the union: both members gain the audit fields, and the status check still narrows to the approved member for approvedBy.
questions.starter:
type Loan = { status: "pending"; amount: number } | { status: "approved"; amount: number; approvedBy: string };

console.log("created 2026-09-20 by app");
questions.expected:
created 2026-09-20 by app
created 2026-09-21 by teller-7, approved by Ngozi

questions.q: Model a booking as a union of held (with expiresAt) and confirmed (with paymentRef), and write summary. Print #1 held until 18:00 and #2 confirmed (PAY-771).
questions.explain: status: string plus optional fields let any mix through. The union ties each field to its state and makes status a real discriminant.

questions.q: Rewrite canWithdraw as an exhaustive switch so that frozen accounts cannot withdraw. Print true false false false for active, dormant, closed and frozen.
questions.explain: Naming every member, and allowing only the one that should be allowed, is "deny by default". With the boolean return type and no default, a fifth status would be a compile error (TS2366).
